title: What are tinnovators?
summary: Josh and Chuck introduce "tinnovators" (rendered in transcript as tentivators/tinovators), people who find new uses for Altoids tins. They open with banter about the Myers-Briggs test, candy eaten during a previous episode, and the history of Altoids (dating to 1780, King George III, curiously strong mints). They discuss Jake von Slat's steampunk copper-plated Altoids tin and its electrochemical etching process, Nick Brand's Altoids-tin flashlights, Aaron Dunlap's USB charger built from a nine-volt battery, Matthew Pogue's speaker and Swiss AVR knife, Limor Fried's Minty Boost, and David Alban's painted tin mosaics. They then read listener mail about why people laugh at America's Funniest Home Videos-style injury clips, and close with plugs for the Facebook pages, the weekly webcast, blogs, and celebrity fans such as Wil Wheaton and Aisha Tyler.

segments.title: Opening banter and Myers-Briggs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the Myers-Briggs personality test and a possible future podcast on it, plus the whale shark idea and the new Altoids articles on the site.

segments.title: Candy during the Twinkies episode and Altoids history
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh address listener questions about candy during the Twinkies episode. They then discuss the Altoids history back to King George III, his porphyria, and the mints' 1780 origins and curiously strong slogan.

segments.title: Kool-Aid vs. Flavor Aid and the Altoids tin
segments.summary: Josh corrects the record that the Jonestown drink was Flavor Aid, not Kool-Aid. They then discuss how people reuse the Altoids tin for storage and crafts, which leads to defining a tinnovator.

segments.title: Jake von Slat and steampunk
segments.summary: The hosts introduce steampunk as a subculture and Jake von Slat as its de facto godfather, who made a steampunk desktop computer and a steampunk Altoids tin. His instructions are shared openly online.

segments.title: Copper-plated etched Altoids tin process
segments.summary: Josh describes Jake von Slat's method: stripping and copper plating the tin with copper sulfate, transferring an etching image, and electrochemically etching it in salt water with a transformer. Josh notes the process is dangerous and that a simpler method was offered.

segments.title: Nick Brand flashlights and Aaron Dunlap USB charger
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Nick Brand's Altoids-tin mini flashlights, which sold widely after appearing on Digg and Boing Boing. They also discuss Aaron Dunlap's nine-volt USB phone charger and the Electroids company he founded.

segments.title: Speakers, Minty Boost, Swiss AVR knife, and artistic tins
segments.summary: The hosts describe Matthew Pogue's Altoids-tin speaker built on Limor Fried's Minty Boost, and his Swiss AVR knife with programmable LEDs and sounds. They then contrast the artistic and technical camps, including David Alban's mosaic-style paintings made from tins. They mention Instructables for more DIY projects.

segments.title: Listener mail: why injury videos are funny
segments.summary: Jason writes in with an excerpt from The Definitive Book of Body Language explaining that the punch line of a joke involving disaster frightens the brain into laughing, which explains why AFV-style injury clips get laughs.

segments.title: Site plugs and celebrity fans
segments.summary: The hosts plug their Facebook pages, the weekly Wednesday webcast, and their blogs. They mention celebrity fans Wil Wheaton and Aisha Tyler and sign off.
